commands.name: harness

commands.name: harness-resume

commands.name: harness-start

commands.name: harness-status

commands.name: harness-stop

commands.name: subagent-task-tree
commands.description: Execute a multi-task implementation plan as a chained subagent tree — you are the parent controller; you spawn one manager per task; each manager spawns a planner, a plan-auditor, one implementer per subtask, per-subtask auditors, and a final drift-auditor. (user)

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify

commands.name: batch

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: built-in-browser

It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify

Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file (one entry per line: date, category, amount, optional note) and is tired of spreadsheets. They need a small tool that reads the file and reports where the money went — usable both from their own Python scripts and from the terminal.

## Solution

A pure-standard-library Python (>= 3.9) package **pennywise**, installable with `pip install .`, that provides:

- a library (`import pennywise`): `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, an `Entry` type and `ParseError`;
- a `pennywise` console command with subcommands `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add`, `export` (also runnable as `python -m pennywise`).

## User Stories

1. As a household bookkeeper, I want to `import pennywise` and call `parse(text)` so that I get typed entries (`date`, `category`, `amount`, `note`) from my ledger.
2. As a bookkeeper, I want a mistake in my file reported with its line number (blank and comment lines counted) so that I can fix it quickly.
3. As a bookkeeper, I want `Rent` and `rent` to be the same category so that my totals are not split by typos in case.
4. As a bookkeeper, I want my balance, per-category totals and per-month totals, both from Python and from the terminal.
5. As a bookkeeper, I want to list entries filtered by category and an inclusive date range, oldest first.
6. As a bookkeeper, I want to append an entry from the terminal, with bad entries refused and my file untouched.
7. As a bookkeeper, I want CSV export and `--json` output so that I can feed other tools.
8. As a bookkeeper, I want `-` to mean standard input so that I can pipe ledgers in.
9. As a scripter, I want reliable exit codes (0 ok, 1 ledger/entry mistake, 2 unreadable file or bad command line).

Layout (src layout, setuptools, no runtime dependencies):

- `src/pennywise/report.py` — `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`.
- `src/pennywise/cli.py` — `main(argv=None) -> int` using `argparse`; `src/pennywise/__main__.py` calls it.

- `ParseError` → `pennywise: line N: <reason>` on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit 1. Output is only written after the whole ledger has parsed.

Prints the added line. `add` does not validate the rest of the existing file. Write failures → exit 2. `-` as FILE for add → exit 2.

- No command / unknown command / bad option → usage on stderr, exit 2.

- Test external behaviour only: the public library API and the CLI via `main(argv)` with captured stdout/stderr (plus a subprocess test of `python -m pennywise`).
- Cover every example from the original request verbatim (the sample ledger gives balance `1457.50`, the summary lines, the `list --category groceries` line).
- Parser: every valid/invalid amount example, invalid date, case folding, note whitespace, comment/blank line counting in error line numbers, too few fields.
- CLI: each subcommand, `--json` shapes, `-` stdin, exit codes 0/1/2, stderr-only on errors, `add` leaving the file byte-identical on refusal, `add` creating a missing file and fixing a missing trailing newline.
- One packaging check: `pip install .` into a temporary venv gives `import pennywise` and a working `pennywise` command (may be a slow/optional test, but must pass in CI-less local runs).

- [ ] `parse(text)` returns entries in file order with `.date` (`datetime.date`), `.category` (lower-case `str`), `.amount` (`Decimal`), `.note` (`str`, `""` when absent).
- [ ] Fields separate on any run of spaces/tabs; the note is the rest of the line, trimmed at both ends only.
- [ ] Amounts: `2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00` equal; `12`, `12.5`, `-0.99` accepted; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc` rejected.
- [ ] Categories are case-insensitive and stored lower-case.
- [ ] Blank lines and `#` comment lines are ignored but counted for line numbers.
- [ ] Any other bad line (including impossible dates like `2024-02-30`) raises `pennywise.ParseError`, a `ValueError` subclass with `.line` = N and a message containing `line N`.
- [ ] `balance` returns the `Decimal` total (zero for no entries); `by_category` / `by_month` (`"YYYY-MM"`) return `dict`s of totals.
- [ ] `filter_entries` filters by case-insensitive category and inclusive `since`/`until`, keeping input order; `None` means no filter.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals (sample ledger → `1457.50`).
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines; default is category.
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since D] [--until D]` prints matching entries oldest first (stable for same day) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` with two-decimal amounts.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends (creating the file if needed) and prints the line in `list` format; an invalid entry is refused and the file is left byte-identical.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `--json` on `balance`, `summary`, `list` prints the specified JSON shapes with amounts as two-decimal strings.
- [ ] `-` as FILE reads the ledger from stdin for every reading command.
- [ ] Exit 0 on success; exit 1 on a ledger/entry mistake with a line-naming message on stderr and empty stdout; exit 2 on unreadable file or bad command line (no/unknown command, bad option value, mistyped `--since`/`--until` date).
- [ ] A stdlib `unittest` suite covers the above and passes.

## Original request

+Pure standard library, Python 3.9 or newer, no third-party packages.
+This installs the importable `pennywise` package and the `pennywise` command
+One entry per line: a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount and an optional note.
+- Fields are separated by any run of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line, trimmed at both ends only.
+- A positive amount is money in, a negative one money out. `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are the same.
+  At most two decimals: `12`, `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5` and `5.` are not.
+- A category is one word: it must not contain any whitespace character (spaces and tabs, but also form feed,
+  vertical tab, no-break space, U+2028 and other Unicode whitespace). `pennywise add` and the file parser
+  apply the same rule, so a line with such a category is an error (exit 1, naming the line).
+- Categories ignore case (`Rent` and `rent` are the same) and are stored in lower case.
+- Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored (but still counted in line numbers).
+- Anything else is a mistake, including dates that do not exist such as `2024-02-30`.

+- A bad line raises `pennywise.ParseError`, a `ValueError` with `.line` (1-based) and a message

+- `balance(entries)` is the `Decimal` total (zero for no entries).
+- `by_category(entries)` and `by_month(entries)` return `dict`s of totals with sorted keys
+- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns matching entries in input
+  order. `category` ignores case; `since` and `until` are `datetime.date` values, both inclusive;
+| `pennywise balance FILE` | total with two decimals |
+| `pennywise summary FILE [--by category\|month]` | `name  total` per group, sorted by name (default `category`) |
+| `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` | matching entries, oldest first (same-day entries keep file order), as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]` |
+| `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` | append an entry (creating the file if needed) and print the line added; an invalid entry is refused and the file is left untouched |
+| `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` | CSV with header `date,category,amount,note`, in `list` order |
+  Amounts are strings with two decimals.
